chapters.title: Chapter 436: Welcome
paragraphs: They stepped fully into the house, and the smell met them as if it had been waiting in the hall.

Savory, deep, the kind of cooking that had taken patience: stewed meat, warm spice, rice that had steamed long enough to perfume the walls. Under it lay bread, or something close to bread, toasted or just broken. The house felt lived-in at once, not staged for guests, only itself, continuing.

The living room opened into the kitchen without a proper door between them. Mrs. Edith stood at the counter with a cloth in her hands and the quiet posture of a woman who had held a household together for years. Mature, kind-faced, a little tired around the eyes. Soft features. Calm presence. She looked up as they came in, and surprise and quiet happiness crossed her expression in the same breath.

"I was wondering what was taking you long to welcome our guests... considering how long you took the last time he visited." Her voice carried mild amusement and genuine affection. "I guessed it to be him, since thesame thing happened last time he visited. Within me, I didn’t expect this guess of mine to be right so soon..."
She smiled, and the tiredness eased.
"Quite the unexpected visit, you two. You’re both welcome."
Sacha moved forward as if the years had been a short walk.
"How have you and Mia been doing, Aunty Edith?"
"We’ve been doing well..." Mrs. Edith set the cloth down. "Well enough. The house still stands. That is something."
Her gaze traveled over Sacha with motherly interest, then shifted to Stan, lingering with a fondness that needed no words.

"Though he visited not too long ago. Looking at you both now, so much more mature..." She smiled softly. "I still find it hard to reconcile that with the memory of your younger selves. But I suppose that is something too. So much time has passed. Sacha, you’re a mature young lady now, so different from the charismatic teenager I remember."
Meanwhile, Mia hovered a half-step behind them, still faintly flushed from the door. She tucked a strand of hair behind her ear and did not quite know where to put her hands.
"Sit," Mrs. Edith said. "Don’t stand there like deliveries. You are not deliveries."

They moved into the living room. The sofa was the same one Stan remembered, only more settled into itself. A photograph on the side table had not changed place: two houses, a strip of fence, children blurred by motion. Sacha noticed it at once.
’I remember when we took that photo...’ Stan shook his head
"And you," Sacha said, softer, "managing here alone. Are you all right? Really."
Mrs. Edith considered the question as if it deserved an honest answer.
"I manage. The house is smaller without certain

noises in it, but it is not empty. Mia is here. That helps more than she thinks." A glance at her daughter. "She has grown into a beautiful young woman. I am allowed to say so. I did some of the work.
Mia made a small sound of protest that was not really protest.
"Aunty," Sacha said, "you’re going to make her hide behind the sofa."
"She can hide after she brings cups." Mrs. Edith was already turning toward the cabinet. "Water? Tea? I have the good leaves, the ones I pretend I am saving."
"Tea," Sacha said. "Please."
Stan added, "Tea is fine."
Mrs. Edith looked at him directly then, fond and faintly teasing.

"Good to see you again so soon. You have a habit of appearing without much warning. I am not complaining. I am observing." She studied his face. "Are you eating? You have that look men get when they think meals are optional. Work too hard and the body sends a bill."
"I’m eating," he said.
"That is what people say while they are not eating." She poured water into the kettle with practiced economy. "I will believe you after you sit at my table."
Stan’s mouth almost smiled. "The food smells good."
"It should. I’m following my usual recipe."

Cups came down. The clink of ceramic was a small, domestic percussion. Mia moved to help, grateful for a task. Her arm brushed Stan’s as she passed; she flushed again and became very interested in saucers.
Sacha, in a lighter register now that Mrs. Edith was present, did not retire her weapons. She only wrapped them in affection.
"The welcome at the door was very thorough, Aunty. We had time to consider our life choices on the step."
Mia’s head came up. "I was opening the door."
"You were conducting a reunion," Sacha said. "With one person. I was scenery."
Mrs. Edith’s mouth twitched. "Some things never change. When you were small, she looked for him first in every room. I used to think she would walk into furniture.
"Mom," Mia said, helpless.
"I am allowed to remember. Memory is free."

Stan stood in the familiar scent of the house and let the talk move around him. It contrasted sharply with the rest of his recent life, the elevator, the red eyes, the ledger of women Sacha did not know how to count. Here the air asked for nothing except presence. Mrs. Edith looked at them both with real warmth. Mia moved softly at the edge of the group, happy in a way that showed in her shoulders more than her mouth.
"How have you been all these years, Sacha?" Mrs. Edith asked. "Still lively? Still sharp-tongued? I used to tell your mother you could cut fruit with that mouth."
"I still can. I use it for love now." Sacha accepted a cup. "Mostly."
"And you two have been taking care of each other?"
"We try," Stan said.
"He forgets to eat," Sacha supplied. "I remind him. He pretends he has a normal face. I correct him."
"That is care," Mrs. Edith decided. "In the local dialect."

They spoke of the old neighborhood without sinking into it: children running between the two houses until the path was a habit; rainy afternoons indoors with the windows pearled and Mrs. Edith’s cooking making the whole block smell claimed; the way the adults had talked over the children’s heads and the children had listened anyway. No one named the man who was missing. The gap sat in the room like a chair no one pulled out, and they left it there.
"You’ll stay for dinner and the night, it’s already late," Mrs. Edith said. It was not quite a question.
Mia looked at Stan, then at Sacha, shy and hopeful. "Will you? There’s enough. There is always enough if she decides there is."
"We will," Sacha said. "He promised me soup with his face."
"I promised nothing of the kind."
"Your face promised. I translated."
Mrs. Edith laughed once, quietly. "Then sit properly. Drinks first. Dinner is almost ready. I will set extra plates. You will not hover in my hallway like people who might flee."

They moved toward the table. Evening light lay along the floor in a long, kind stripe. The kettle clicked off. Steam rose. Mia set cups down with care, still a little pink, still glancing at Stan as if the hug at the door had not finished happening.
Mrs. Edith placed a hand briefly on Sacha’s shoulder, then on the back of Stan’s chair as he sat.
"Welcome home for the evening," she said. "Eat. Talk. The house likes voices."

chapters.title: Chapter 437: Catching Up With Mia
paragraphs: Mrs. Edith set her cup down and turned toward the stove, the evening already gathering itself back into pots and timing.
Sacha pouted, playful, exaggerated.
"Do you think Mia still likes me? With her giving Stan her Stan all the hug outside..."
Mrs. Edith laughed softly, eyes warm. "She’s always had a soft side for Stan..."
Sacha knew that. She had known it since cardboard houses and paper hundreds. She said it anyway, to put a little more air into a room that still remembered absences.
Mrs. Edith glanced toward the sofa. "Mia. Come help me finish this."
Mia’s hands tightened on her sleeve. Before she could stand, Sacha was up.
"Why does Mia need to help you when I’m here? Let the girl rest for a while. I’ll help you in the kitchen with whatever you need..."
Mrs. Edith shrugged, smiling. "Okay..."
They walked out together. At the kitchen threshold Sacha looked back and winked, quick, conspiratorial, meant for one person only.
Stan caught it and smiled to himself.
’Nice one, Sacha...’

She teased without mercy and still cleared the room for him. In a life crowded with claims and careful distances, that kind of loyalty was rare. It warmed his chest in a simple way. No ledger. No repayment in cultivation resources. Just his sister making space and trusting him to use it.
Pots resumed. A cupboard. Water running. The living room softened around the two of them. Evening light lay along the floor in a long stripe. The stew’s scent drifted in, distant now, comforting.
Stan’s gaze shifted to Mia.

She sat close enough that the cushion remembered both of them. What he did not see was the work it took her to stay that way. The hug at the door had left heat under her skin and the faint trace of him in her breathing. Old familiarity pulled at her shoulder, at her hands, at the small gap of fabric and air between hip and hip. Her body wanted to close it, lean, tuck, rest her temple where it used to belong when they were smaller and no one called it anything. She kept her hands in her lap. Her heart did not cooperate.
He turned toward her fully.
"What’s up?" Easy. Unhurried. "You look like you’re holding something in."
Mia glanced toward the kitchen, then back. "I’m not. I’m just glad you’re here." A breath. "Properly here. Not in a crowd."
"How have you been?" he asked. "Since the match. That’s the last time we actually talked. Peak and Crown. After the noise died down."

The gym came back in pieces: varnish and dust, the squeak of shoes, Peak taking the night because he had made it take the night. Velaris Crown colors in the stands. Finding her afterward at the edge of the thinning noise. A short conversation. Then the road.

"The rest of that day felt strange," Mia said. "You won. People were loud in the corridors. I walked back to campus with two girls from my year who kept asking if I knew you, and I said yes, and then I didn’t know how to add the rest without sounding like I was making a claim." She smiled, small. "I sat in my room and replayed the two minutes we had. That’s embarrassing to admit."
"It isn’t."

"It is a little." Her fingers smoothed the seam of her sleeve and stopped. "After that, Crown just... continued. Lectures. Group work that never ends when it should. A friend who cries about internships in the library as if the building is a confessional. I still go to some games. Not all. When Peak is on the sheet I look, even if I’m supposed to be loyal to the wrong side." A quiet laugh. "I tell myself I’m scouting. I’m not scouting."
"And home?"

"Aunty keeps the house standing and help where I can." The joke was soft. Under it: "It’s quieter than it used to be. Not empty. Quieter. Last week when you came, the quiet changed shape for a few hours. I didn’t realize how much I had been walking around inside it until you were at the door."
Stan listened. He always had, with her. It was one of the things that made the attention feel heavier than it looked.
"Anything major change?" he asked. "Time is long when you’re in them.

Mia thought. "Nothing that would sound major to anyone else. I sleep better some days. Worse others. I cook on the nights Mom is tired, and she pretends she isn’t grateful. I think about the old street more than I say out loud." She looked at him. "You?"

"Busy," he said, and left the shape of busy packed. "School. Moving between places. Eating when Sacha reminds me." A faint dry note. "Sitting in this house again feels strange. And good. Like the furniture kept our places."
"It did." Mia’s voice thinned with something fond. "I was nervous when I opened the door. Then I wasn’t. Then Sacha was there and I was nervous again for a different reason."
"She likes you."
"She likes teasing me. That’s her dialect for liking me." Mia’s mouth curved. "I missed that dialect."

A comfortable silence opened. Kitchen sounds stitched it, Sacha asking where something lived, Mrs. Edith answering without looking. Mia’s shoulder drifted half an inch toward him and halted. Heat from his arm reached her sleeve. She did not take the last inch.

"When I saw you last week," she said, quieter, "I wanted to say I’d been fine and also that I hadn’t, and neither sentence was the whole thing. So I hugged you instead. That wasn’t a strategy. It was the only complete sentence I had."
Stan’s mouth almost smiled. "It landed."

"Good." Color touched her cheeks again. She almost set her hand on his forearm, the old reflex, the childhood one, and caught herself, fingers curling back into her palm. "Don’t tell Sacha I said any of this. She’ll put it on a banner."
"I won’t."
"You might. You have that calm face that means you’re filing things."
"I’m just listening."
"That’s worse." But she was happy when she said it.

chapters.title: Chapter 438: Dinner
paragraphs: The kitchen grew busier while they talked. Lids tapped against pots, plates stacked, and water ran briefly in the sink before stopping again.
From the next room, Sacha’s voice carried as she rummaged through cupboards, asking where the good bowls were as if the house had been waiting all this time for her to remember it.
She appeared a moment later with a stack of dishes balanced in both hands, wearing the confidence of someone who had appointed herself staff years ago and never quite resigned.
"Move," she ordered cheerfully.
Stan shifted his chair.
"Not you. The plates."
"Ah."

Sacha set the dishes down one by one and began serving without waiting for permission. She placed a generous portion in front of Stan, another in front of Mia, and only then helped herself, as if to prevent anyone from accusing her of neglecting her own plate. Steam rose immediately.
The stew arrived whole, the meat, the spices, the deep savory scent of something that had simmered long enough for every ingredient to surrender its stubbornness and agree to become dinner.
She sat with a satisfied sigh and looked between Stan and Mia, her mouth slowly curling into a pout. "You two have probably forgotten I even exist now that you’ve had some alone time together."
Stan only smiled, calm and unbothered, as if the accusation were weather he had already dressed for. Mia looked down at her plate. Color climbed her cheeks as though the ceramic had given it to her.
"And you looked so quiet when I walked in," Sacha continued, delighted. "Cozy. Peaceful. Like I interrupted a very important private meeting."
"We were just talking," Mia said.
"To him?"
Mia hesitated.
Sacha gasped softly. "How scandalous."
Mia gave her an embarrassed look, and Sacha laughed. "Relax. I’m teasing." She picked up her spoon, then glanced at Stan again. "Besides, you have that look."
"What look?"
"The one you get when you’re pretending nothing happened."
"Nothing happened."
"Exactly."
Mrs. Edith followed only seconds later with more dishes, rice, bread, vegetables, and another bowl that smelled of spice and time. "Make room," she said.
The table filled quickly. Steam braided itself through the warm light. Chairs scraped against the floor. Someone passed a napkin that did not belong to them, and no one bothered correcting it.

"Eat properly," Mrs. Edith said as she finally sat down. "Not like people grazing at a train station. Sit. Pass the food. And thank the cook, even if one of you helped and will try to claim half the credit."
Sacha placed a hand over her chest. "I stirred. Stirring is half the work."
"You asked where the salt was twice."
"I was supervising."
"You were standing beside the salt."
Sacha paused. "That was strategic supervision."
Mrs. Edith smiled. "One quarter, if I am generous."
Stan chuckled, and Sacha pointed at him at once. "Don’t laugh. You benefited from my labor."
"I know.
"Good."

They settled into their places: Mrs. Edith in her familiar seat, Sacha opposite her already wearing the expression of someone preparing to cause trouble, Stan and Mia close enough that their plates seemed to belong to the same conversation. For a few moments nobody spoke. Then utensils found work, and the first mouthfuls made conversation wait, briefly, out of respect.
Mia was the first to break the silence. "This tastes like home."
Stan nodded after another bite. "It’s good."
Mrs. Edith looked at him with a teasing smile. "Just good?"
Despite knowing she was only teasing him, he corrected himself immediately. "Better than good."
"That sounds more respectful." She returned to her meal. "Eat more than compliments. Compliments don’t fill a plate."
Sacha pointed her fork toward the stew. "I chopped."
"You chopped one onion."
"A very important onion."
"That onion would have been chopped whether you were there or not."
"It cried for me."
"The onion cries for everyone," Mrs. Edith replied. "Do not make it personal."

Laughter loosened the table. Dishes moved from hand to hand, rice, meat that had long since surrendered its stubbornness, bread torn apart and shared without ceremony. The house seemed to lean in around the four of them, as if it remembered this arrangement and approved.

After a few more bites, Mrs. Edith looked at Sacha over the rim of her cup. "And you? How have you been all these years? How’s work? Have you been keeping yourself out of trouble? Made any new friends? Met anyone interesting?"
Sacha chewed thoughtfully before swallowing. "Work has been... work."
"That means trouble."
"It means previous trouble."
Mrs. Edith raised an eyebrow.
Sacha smiled. "I’ve had a few jobs."
"A few?"
"Yes."
"How many is a few?"
"Depends on whether we’re counting the ones I quit before they could fire me."
Stan lowered his eyes to his plate, hiding a smile. Mia noticed.
"You already know about this?"
"Some of it," Stan said.
"Of course he does," Sacha said. "He has an annoying habit of knowing things."
Mrs. Edith leaned forward slightly. "Well?"

Sacha shrugged. "My first proper job after leaving school was at a small accounting firm. Nothing glamorous. Mostly invoices, payroll, reports, chasing people who owed money, and fixing mistakes other people insisted weren’t mistakes."
"That sounds familiar," Stan murmured.

Sacha ignored him. "The work itself wasn’t bad. I actually liked it. The people were decent enough, too. But my supervisor had this wonderful philosophy that if a problem wasn’t noticed by the client, it wasn’t a problem.
Mrs. Edith frowned. "That sounds dangerous."
"It was."
"What happened?"
"I found an error in one of the quarterly reports. It wasn’t huge, but it would have caused a client to overpay by a fairly embarrassing amount."
"And?"
"I pointed it out." Sacha paused dramatically. "My supervisor told me to leave it."
Mia looked up. "You didn’t."
"Of course I didn’t."
Stan smiled faintly as Sacha continued. "So I corrected it myself and sent the proper figures to the client."
"And your supervisor?"
"Angry."
"Very?"
"He called me disrespectful."
Mrs. Edith shook her head. Sacha grinned. "I told him respecting his position didn’t mean respecting a mistake."
Stan coughed into his cup. Mia laughed. Mrs. Edith gave Sacha a look that was half amusement and half warning.
"You always had a sharp tongue."
"I’ve improved."
"You have not."
"Thank you."
"That wasn’t praise."
"I’ll take it anyway." Sacha tore off a piece of bread. "That job lasted eight months."
"And the next?"
"Customer service."
Mrs. Edith blinked. "You?"
"Yes, me."
"How long?"
"Six months."
"What happened?"
"I discovered that customers are not always right."
Mrs. Edith sighed. "Sacha."
"I know, I know. That’s apparently not something you’re supposed to say aloud."

sentences.text: The kitchen grew busier while they talked.
Lids tapped against pots, plates stacked, and water ran briefly in the sink before stopping again.
From the next room, Sacha’s voice carried as she rummaged through cupboards, asking where the good bowls were as if the house had been waiting all this time for her to remember it.
She appeared a moment later with a stack of dishes balanced in both hands, wearing the confidence of someone who had appointed herself staff years ago and never quite resigned.
"Move," she ordered cheerfully.
Stan shifted his chair.
"Not you.
The plates."
"Ah."
Sacha set the dishes down one by one and began serving without waiting for permission.
She placed a generous portion in front of Stan, another in front of Mia, and only then helped herself, as if to prevent anyone from accusing her of neglecting her own plate.
Steam rose immediately.
The stew arrived whole, the meat, the spices, the deep savory scent of something that had simmered long enough for every ingredient to surrender its stubbornness and agree to become dinner.
She sat with a satisfied sigh and looked between Stan and Mia, her mouth slowly curling into a pout.
"You two have probably forgotten I even exist now that you’ve had some alone time together."
Stan only smiled, calm and unbothered, as if the accusation were weather he had already dressed for.
Mia looked down at her plate.
Color climbed her cheeks as though the ceramic had given it to her.
"And you looked so quiet when I walked in," Sacha continued, delighted.
"Cozy.
Peaceful.
Like I interrupted a very important private meeting."
"We were just talking," Mia said.
"To him?"
Mia hesitated.
Sacha gasped softly.
"How scandalous."
Mia gave her an embarrassed look, and Sacha laughed.
"Relax.
I’m teasing." She picked up her spoon, then glanced at Stan again.
"Besides, you have that look."
"What look?"
"The one you get when you’re pretending nothing happened."
"Nothing happened."
"Exactly."
Mrs.
Edith followed only seconds later with more dishes, rice, bread, vegetables, and another bowl that smelled of spice and time.
"Make room," she said.
The table filled quickly.
Steam braided itself through the warm light.
Chairs scraped against the floor.
Someone passed a napkin that did not belong to them, and no one bothered correcting it.
"Eat properly," Mrs.
Edith said as she finally sat down.
"Not like people grazing at a train station.
Sit.
Pass the food.
And thank the cook, even if one of you helped and will try to claim half the credit."
Sacha placed a hand over her chest.
"I stirred.
Stirring is half the work."
"You asked where the salt was twice."
"I was supervising."
"You were standing beside the salt."
Sacha paused.
"That was strategic supervision."
Mrs.
Edith smiled.
"One quarter, if I am generous."
Stan chuckled, and Sacha pointed at him at once.
"Don’t laugh.
You benefited from my labor."
"I know.
"Good."
They settled into their places: Mrs.

Edith in her familiar seat, Sacha opposite her already wearing the expression of someone preparing to cause trouble, Stan and Mia close enough that their plates seemed to belong to the same conversation.
For a few moments nobody spoke.
Then utensils found work, and the first mouthfuls made conversation wait, briefly, out of respect.
Mia was the first to break the silence.
"This tastes like home."
Stan nodded after another bite.
"It’s good."
Mrs.
Edith looked at him with a teasing smile.
"Just good?"
Despite knowing she was only teasing him, he corrected himself immediately.
"Better than good."
"That sounds more respectful." She returned to her meal.
"Eat more than compliments.
Compliments don’t fill a plate."
Sacha pointed her fork toward the stew.
"I chopped."
"You chopped one onion."
"A very important onion."
"That onion would have been chopped whether you were there or not."
"It cried for me."
"The onion cries for everyone," Mrs.
Edith replied.
"Do not make it personal."
Laughter loosened the table.
Dishes moved from hand to hand, rice, meat that had long since surrendered its stubbornness, bread torn apart and shared without ceremony.
The house seemed to lean in around the four of them, as if it remembered this arrangement and approved.
After a few more bites, Mrs.
Edith looked at Sacha over the rim of her cup.
"And you?
How have you been all these years?
How’s work?
Have you been keeping yourself out of trouble?
Made any new friends?
Met anyone interesting?"
Sacha chewed thoughtfully before swallowing.
"Work has been... work."
"That means trouble."
"It means previous trouble."
Mrs.
Edith raised an eyebrow.
Sacha smiled.
"I’ve had a few jobs."
"A few?"
"Yes."
"How many is a few?"
"Depends on whether we’re counting the ones I quit before they could fire me."
Stan lowered his eyes to his plate, hiding a smile.
Mia noticed.
"You already know about this?"
"Some of it," Stan said.
"Of course he does," Sacha said.
"He has an annoying habit of knowing things."
Mrs.
Edith leaned forward slightly.
"Well?"
Sacha shrugged.
"My first proper job after leaving school was at a small accounting firm.
Nothing glamorous.
Mostly invoices, payroll, reports, chasing people who owed money, and fixing mistakes other people insisted weren’t mistakes."
"That sounds familiar," Stan murmured.
Sacha ignored him.
"The work itself wasn’t bad.
I actually liked it.
The people were decent enough, too.
But my supervisor had this wonderful philosophy that if a problem wasn’t noticed by the client, it wasn’t a problem.
Mrs.
Edith frowned.
"That sounds dangerous."
"It was."
"What happened?"
"I found an error in one of the quarterly reports.
It wasn’t huge, but it would have caused a client to overpay by a fairly embarrassing amount."
"And?"
"I pointed it out." Sacha paused dramatically.
"My supervisor told me to leave it."
Mia looked up.
"You didn’t."
"Of course I didn’t."
Stan smiled faintly as Sacha continued.
"So I corrected it myself and sent the proper figures to the client."
"And your supervisor?"
"Angry."
"Very?"
"He called me disrespectful."
Mrs.
Edith shook her head.
Sacha grinned.
"I told him respecting his position didn’t mean respecting a mistake."
Stan coughed into his cup.
Mia laughed.
Mrs.
Edith gave Sacha a look that was half amusement and half warning.
"You always had a sharp tongue."
"I’ve improved."
"You have not."
"Thank you."
"That wasn’t praise."
"I’ll take it anyway." Sacha tore off a piece of bread.
"That job lasted eight months."
"And the next?"
"Customer service."
Mrs.
Edith blinked.
"You?"
"Yes, me."
"How long?"
"Six months."
"What happened?"
"I discovered that customers are not always right."
Mrs.
Edith sighed.
"Sacha."
"I know, I know.
That’s apparently not something you’re supposed to say aloud."

chapters.title: Chapter 439: Road To Management
paragraphs: "I discovered that customers are not always right."
Mrs. Edith sighed. "Sacha."
"I know, I know. That’s apparently not something you’re supposed to say aloud."
"What did you do?"
"Corrected a customer."
"How?"
"Politely."
Stan raised an eyebrow. Sacha pointed at him at once. "I was polite."
"I believe you."
"You don’t sound like you believe me."
"I believe you were polite by your standards."
Mia covered a smile. Sacha shook her head and continued.
"Anyway, that job wasn’t terrible. I learned a lot. Handling people, managing complaints, keeping calm when someone is shouting over something they don’t understand. It was useful."
"You kept those skills?" Mrs. Edith asked.

"Obviously. They’re one of the reasons I’m doing well as a manager now. If not for them I would have run the company into bankruptcy." Her gaze shifted to Stan as she said it, and that earned a small smile from Mrs. Edith.
Sacha continued eating for a moment before adding, "Then came the one that nearly killed my patience."
"The company you’re with now?" Mia asked.
"No. Before that." Sacha leaned back. "I joined a mid-sized company. Good salary. Decent position. Plenty of room to grow."
"And the boss?"
Sacha’s expression changed. "He was the problem."
Stan finally looked up. Mia noticed the slight shift in his face.

Sacha sighed. "He wasn’t just incompetent. That would’ve been easier. He was annoying." Mrs. Edith waited, and Sacha pushed on. "He took credit for other people’s work. Played favorites. Made promises to clients without consulting anyone. Then when those promises became impossible to keep, he’d dump the mess on whoever was beneath him."
"That sounds unpleasant," Mia said.
"It was exhausting."
"You argued with him?" Mrs. Edith asked.
"Sometimes."
"Of course."

Sacha sighed and pushed a piece of meat around her plate. "He was a terrible manager, honestly. He kept piling work on me because he knew I could handle it. I’d finish one thing, and he’d immediately hand me three more. Late nights became normal. Weekends too, sometimes.
Mrs. Edith’s expression tightened. "He was overworking you?"
"Constantly. And the worst part was that he wasn’t even doing his own job properly."
"How so?"

"The company’s stock had been falling for months. Investors were losing confidence, sales were slipping, and instead of actually fixing anything, he kept making bad decisions and pretending everything was under control." Stan listened quietly while Sacha went on. "He’d ignore reports he didn’t like, dismiss warnings from the finance team, and push strategies that clearly weren’t working. Then he’d blame the market whenever the numbers got worse."
Mrs. Edith frowned. "And you told him?"
"More than once."
"And what did he say?"
"That I should focus on my own department and leave management to him." Sacha gave a dry laugh. "Which would have been easier if he hadn’t kept dumping his work on me."
Stan chuckled quietly.
Sacha pointed at him. "Don’t laugh. You weren’t the one answering emails at eleven at night because your boss suddenly remembered a report existed."
"I remember you telling me about that."

"Exactly." She turned back to Mrs. Edith. "I wasn’t even angry about the workload at first. I was angry because I knew the company could do better. People were working hard, but the man at the top kept making decisions that were dragging everyone down."
"And that’s when Stan stepped in?"
"Eventually." Sacha glanced at Stan. "He looked into what was happening, saw how badly the company was being managed, and apparently decided he’d had enough."
Stan shrugged. "He was costing the company money."
"And overworking me."
"That too."
Sacha smiled. "That’s how I ended up becoming manager."
Mrs. Edith looked between them. "So you went from being overworked by him to replacing him?"
"Pretty much." She lifted her cup. "Best promotion I’ve ever received."
"So that’s one of the companies under him?" Mia said softly.
Sacha nodded. "Yeah." She lifted her cup again. "The manager absolutely deserved it." Then she set it down. "To be fair, Stan didn’t simply walk in and fire him because I complained."
"I would have liked to," Stan said.
"I know." Sacha’s smile softened. "But the man had already been doing stupid things. Stan just happened to uncover enough of them to make sure the company couldn’t ignore it anymore."
Mrs. Edith looked impressed. "And after that?"
Sacha grinned. "They offered me his position."
Mia blinked. "You became the manager?"
"Yep."
"Just like that?"

"While under Stan’s order the job’s technically mine. There were interviews, meetings, paperwork, and several people suddenly discovering that I was apparently qualified to do the job I’d already been doing for months.
Stan nodded. "They were slow to notice."
"Very slow." Sacha leaned back proudly. "But eventually they noticed."
Mrs. Edith smiled. "And you like it?"

Sacha’s expression became more genuine. "I do." The answer came without hesitation. "I actually do. It’s stressful, but it’s different when you’re the one making the decisions. I can change things instead of complaining about them. I can protect the people working under me from some of the nonsense I had to deal with."
Mrs. Edith nodded approvingly. "Then it sounds like you found your place."
"Maybe." Sacha looked down at her plate. "I still complain."
"That’s because you’re you."
"Exactly."
Stan smiled. Sacha glanced at him. "And don’t think I’ve forgotten that you’re partly responsible."
"For what?"
"My promotion."
"You earned it."
"Maybe. But you opened the door."
Stan shrugged. "You walked through it."
For once, Sacha didn’t have a clever response. She simply smiled.
Mia watched the exchange quietly, then passed Sacha the bread. Sacha accepted it.
"Thank you."
"You’re welcome."
A beat passed. Then Sacha’s eyes narrowed playfully. "See? Mia appreciates me."
"I never said I didn’t."
"You implied it."
"I did not."
"You did with your face."
"My face doesn’t speak."
"But it does when you’re around him."
Mia nearly choked on her drink. Stan calmly continued eating. Mrs. Edith shook her head.
"Leave her a little pride, Sacha. She has to swallow food as well as your comments."

chapters.title: Chapter 440: Nothing Needed Fixing
paragraphs: Sacha talked about the people she had met, the employees she now managed, the ridiculous problems that somehow became emergencies at five minutes before closing, and the strange talent some people possessed for sending messages marked URGENT when the issue could have waited until morning.
She talked about the little victories too.
An employee she’d helped gain confidence. A project that had nearly collapsed but somehow came together.
The first time someone had come to her for advice rather than simply following an instruction.
Those were the moments she seemed proudest of.
Mrs. Edith listened closely. "And outside work?"
Sacha shrugged. "I’m alive."
"That isn’t an answer."
"Fine. I’ve made friends. Lost touch with some people. Kept in touch with others. I’ve gone out. I’ve traveled a little. Nothing dramatic."
"Anyone special?"
Sacha immediately looked at her. "Ah."
Mrs. Edith smiled innocently. "I was only asking."
"You were absolutely not only asking."
Mia lowered her head, suddenly very interested in her rice.
Stan said nothing, but had a slight smile on his face, he watched as Sacha looked around the table before saying, "No."
Mrs. Edith waited. "No what?"
"No one special."
"Not even anyone interesting?"
"Interesting people are dangerous."
Stan nodded. "That’s true."
Sacha pointed at him. "You’re not helping."
Mrs. Edith chuckled. "Well, as long as you’re happy."
"I am."
"And taking care of yourself?"
"Mostly."
"Mostly, just that?"
"I sleep."
"How much?"
Sacha hesitated.
Mrs. Edith immediately knew. "Sacha."
"Enough sleep, ."
"That is not a number."
"Six hours sometimes."
Mrs. Edith frowned. "Try seven."
"I’ll try."
"Try harder."
"Yes, ma’am." Sacha smiled and returned to her food.
For a while, they spoke of the old homw in passing—the path worn between houses, rainy windows, children who had once treated two kitchens as one.

Stan ate more than he had expected to. He offered short answers when Sacha pulled him into conversations, smiled whenever she circled back to the hug at the doorway as though it were a seasonal topic.
Mia remained soft-spoken, her color rising and fading whenever Sacha teased her, but she was comfortable enough that she occasionally forgot to guard herself.
She laughed at Sacha’s imitation of her former manager.
She smiled at Mrs. Edith’s dry corrections. She leaned slightly toward Stan without realizing it.
And every so often, when she thought no one was looking, she simply looked around the table.
Four people, warm food. Familiar voices. For once, nothing needed fixing. Utensils clicked. Steam thinned.
Second helpings appeared because Mrs. Edith decided they would.
"More?" she asked Stan.
"A little."
"A little is how men say yes."
She served him anyway.
Sacha leaned back, satisfied. "See? The house still works."
She gestured around the table. "Four plates. Too much food. Me, unappreciated. Perfect."
"You’re appreciated," Mia said.
Sacha immediately pointed at her. "Say it while looking at me."
Mia looked up, smiling helplessly. "You’re appreciated."
"Better."
Sacha lifted her cup. "To existing. I was worried."
Mrs. Edith’s laugh was quiet. Outside, evening thickened against the windows.
Inside, the conversation settled into a lull that didn’t feel like an ending.
Only a breath between mouthfuls. The table held them the way it had been built to—warm, ordinary, and full.

They soon finished eating. Mia stood first and began packing the dishes, stacking plates with care. Utensils gathered in her other hand. The table looked suddenly larger without the work of food on it.
Mrs. Edith watched her for a moment, then turned to Sacha.
"You’ll be all right sleeping with Mia in her room? Stan can take the guest room."
Sacha did not hesitate. "I’m fine with it. Why would I have a problem with that?"
Mrs. Edith’s mouth eased, as if a small household equation had balanced.
"I didn’t want to just eat and sit," Sacha added. "I’ll help Mia wash up."
"You’ve already helped with the cooking," Mrs. Edith said, gentle, already tired in the kind way. "You don’t need to stress yourself further."
"I do, actually. That’s the point."
Stan, who had been listening without inserting himself, spoke then. "I’ll help too."

Mrs. Edith looked at the three of them and knew she was outnumbered. The sigh she gave was fond and defeated in equal measure. These two—children she had long regarded as almost her own—were determined to help her daughter with the dishes. She could not refuse them.
"Go on, then. The sink doesn’t negotiate."

They took the stacks through. The kitchen still smelled of stew and spice; heat lingered above the stove. Water ran. Plates found a rhythm: Mia rinsing, Stan washing with calm efficiency, Sacha drying and setting things in the rack as if she had never left the geography of this particular counter.
"You missed a spot," Sacha said, not meaning it.
Stan turned the plate under the tap. "I didn’t."
"I know. I just like the sound of management."
Mia smiled at the sink. "Thank you. Both of you. I usually do this part alone and pretend it’s meditation."
"It’s not meditation," Sacha said. "It’s dishes. Don’t give porcelain a spiritual life."

A glass clinked against another. Water drummed the basin. Mia’s shoulder brushed Stan’s as she passed him a bowl; she murmured sorry and did not look sorry. Sacha noticed, of course, and only hummed, a soft tease without teeth.
"Some teams never change their positions."
"Sis."
"I’m drying. I’m allowed commentary."
Mrs. Edith appeared once in the doorway, cloth in hand, then left them to it, her weary affection hanging in the air like the last of the steam.
They finished quickly. Coordination did that. The counter came clean. The rack filled. The tap shut off and left a dripping quiet that felt like a completed sentence.
Stan dried his hands.
"I’ll take the guest room," he said. "Good night. Thank you for dinner."
"Sleep," Mrs. Edith answered from the hall. "Goodnight. Have a good sleep, see you in the morning Stan."

chapters.title: Chapter 450: Where We Still Belong
paragraphs: Stan soon slept off, he didn’t know how long had passed but he woke up not too long after...

Morning had taken the amber out of the room. What came through the curtains now was pale and honest, the kind of light that made last night sit differently in the body, less fever, more fact. The other side of the bed was empty. The sheet there was cool. He put his palm on it for a second, as if warmth might still be hiding in the cotton, then let the hand fall.

Recollection arrived without drama. The door. Her silhouette. The lie of sleep. Her mouth. The careful way he had gone into her, and the way she had said his name when she came. He sat up slowly, elbows on his knees, and let it settle.
No regret. A quiet, startled tenderness, and under it the simple knowledge that the girl who used to wait on the porch steps was not a girl he could pretend not to see anymore.

He dressed without hurry. Shirt. Jeans. The guest-room floor was cool under his feet. In the hallway the house smelled like oil and onions and something sweet underneath, bread, maybe, or fruit going into a pan. He followed it the way you follow a voice you trust.

The kitchen was already a living thing. Mrs. Edith at the stove, spatula ticking against a pan. Mia at the counter tearing herbs with her fingers, hair tied up in a way that left the back of her neck bare. Sacha in a chair with one foot tucked under her, stealing a piece of something fried and hissing when it burned her tongue. Sunlight laid a clean stripe across the table. Plates waited in a stack. A kettle clicked off and nobody jumped; they knew the sound.
"Morning," Stan said.
Three faces turned. Mrs. Edith’s smile arrived first, wide and unperformed. "There he is. Sit before Sacha finishes the eggs."
"I heard that," Sacha said, and then, milder, "Hi."

Mia said his name like a small, private fact. "Stan." Her eyes flicked to his and away, a blush climbing that had nothing to do with the stove. He answered her with a look that stayed gentle and did not advertise anything, and she went back to the herbs with more concentration than herbs required.

They sat. The meal was the kind that makes a table feel like a place instead of furniture: eggs still steaming, bread with a brown crust, tomatoes bright with salt, a pot of tea that Mrs. Edith kept refilling without asking who wanted more. Utensils chimed. Someone’s chair scraped. Sacha talked with her mouth half full and Mrs. Edith pretended to scold her and did not mean it.
"You sleep all right?" Mrs. Edith asked Stan, already pouring.
"Yes. Thank you. The room’s kind."
"It’s been kind to a lot of people." She set the pot down. "Eat. You’re too thin for a boy who works as much as Sacha says you do."
Sacha snorted. "He isn’t a boy when the invoices come."
"He’s a boy at my table," Mrs. Edith said, and that was the end of that branch of the subject.

Conversation wandered the way good breakfast conversation does. A neighbor’s dog. A market price that had gone stupid. Whether the rainy season would start on time. Mia mentioned a lecture she was dreading and Sacha offered, with great generosity, to suffer it in her place and take the credit.

Stan listened more than he spoke, which was his habit in this house, and when he did speak it was small, complimenting the bread, asking Mrs. Edith if the garden out back still fought her in the dry months. She laughed and said the garden had never respected anyone, including God.
Mia’s glances kept arriving like birds that did not quite land. When their knees almost touched under the table she went still, then pretended to reach for the jam. He let her have the pretense.
The afterglow did not need an audience. It lived well enough in the way she passed him the tea without being asked, and in the way he took it.
Mrs. Edith rose to fetch more bread from the kitchen. The moment the doorway swallowed her, Sacha leaned in, voice low enough to be a conspiracy and bright enough to be a joke.
"Guest room was very quiet," she said. "Either you two prayed all night or you learned how not to make the bed creak."
Stan’s mouth did the calm thing it did when he was being hunted for sport. "We slept."

"Mm." Sacha’s eyes cut to Mia, who had become extremely interested in a crust. "She’s been looking at you like you invented morning. And you look like a man who remembers something and is trying not to smile about it.
"Eat your eggs, Sacha."
"That’s not a no."
It was not a yes either. He drank his tea. Mia’s ears were pink. Sacha sat back, satisfied with the damage, and stole another tomato as a victory tax.

Mrs. Edith returned, the teasing folded itself away, and the meal ran down into the comfortable work of being finished, plates stacked, cups emptied, the last piece of bread claimed by no one and then by Sacha after a decent interval.
When the table had been cleared enough to feel like a table again, Stan stayed in his chair a moment longer.
"Auntie."
Mrs. Edith looked up, drying her hands on a cloth.
"I’d like to send you some money," he said. No flourish. "Not as a bill. As thanks. For me. For Sacha. For all you’ve done for the two of us."
She was already shaking her head before he finished. "No. There is no difference between you three in my heart. You, Sacha, Mia, my children. You don’t pay a mother for feeding her own."
He listened all the way through. Then he nodded, as if he had expected the refusal and respected it, and still would not let it be the last word.
"I’m not trying to settle a debt," he said. "I want to help. If there’s anything. Anything at all."
The cloth in her hands slowed. The kitchen sounds, the tap, a distant bird, Sacha pretending not to listen, filled the pause.
